Maker
MAY-ker
n.
From make, Old English macian. Webster 1828: the Creator; and, in a lower sense, one who makes or forms. Applied to God the word is a title of right — the one who made a thing has a claim on it — and the Authorized Version uses it where that claim is being pressed.

Biblical Definition

Maker in Scripture is a title that settles arguments. Eliphaz asks Job, shall a man be more pure than his maker? (Job 4:17), and Elihu will not flatter because my maker would soon take me away (Job 32:22). The psalm makes it the ground of worship: O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker (Psalm 95:6) — posture follows from origin. Proverbs makes it the ground of social duty, twice: He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker (Proverbs 14:31) and Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker (Proverbs 17:5). The reason is given plainly: The rich and poor meet together: the LORD is the maker of them all (Proverbs 22:2). Isaiah turns the title into the tenderest metaphor in the prophets: thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name (Isaiah 54:5). And Hebrews sets it at the end of Abraham’s looking: he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God (Hebrews 11:10). The word therefore grounds worship, ethics, marriage, and hope in a single fact — that we did not make ourselves.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines MAKER as the Creator — a title given to God by way of eminence — and, secondarily, one who forms, shapes, or fabricates anything. The theological weight lies in the right of the one who made.

expand to see more

MAKER, n. — The Creator. God is called the Maker of all things, and the title belongs to Him by way of eminence.

One who makes, forms, shapes or moulds; a manufacturer; as, a maker of cloth.

One who writes verses; a poet — an older English sense, now obsolete.

Webster puts the divine sense first, and rightly. In English the word can name a craftsman, but in Scripture it names a right: the one who made a thing may dispose of it, and the creature owes Him worship because of what he is, not merely because of what he has received.

Key Scripture

Job 4:17 — "Shall mortal man be more just than God? shall a man be more pure than his maker?"

Psalm 95:6 — "O come, let us worship and bow down: let us kneel before the LORD our maker."

Proverbs 14:31 — "He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the poor."

Isaiah 54:5 — "For thy Maker is thine husband; the LORD of hosts is his name; and thy Redeemer the Holy One of Israel; The God of the whole earth shall he be called."

Hebrews 11:10 — "For he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God."

Modern Corruption

The title is emptied by any account of origins that removes a Maker — and with Him the ground Proverbs gives for honouring the poor, since the argument there is not shared humanity in the abstract but a shared Maker.

expand to see more

Proverbs 14:31 and 17:5 do not argue from dignity as a self-evident property. They argue from a Maker: to oppress or mock the poor is to reproach the One who made him. Remove the Maker and the argument has no premise left, whatever sentiment survives it. This is why the Christian case for the worth of every human being cannot be borrowed from the age’s vocabulary and must be preached from Genesis 1:27 and Proverbs 22:2. The rich and poor meet together: the LORD is the maker of them all is a sentence about creation before it is a sentence about ethics, and the ethics will not stand without it.

Psalm 95:6 shows the same structure in worship. The reason to kneel is that He is the LORD our maker, and the psalm goes on immediately to the warning about hardening the heart as at Meribah. Worship offered on any other ground — because it is meaningful, because it is moving, because it is our tradition — is worship resting on the worshipper. Isaiah 54:5 then adds the astonishment: the Maker is also the husband. The God who has the absolute right of a Creator over His creature has bound Himself to her by covenant, and the second fact does not cancel the first but makes it bearable.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew is the participle 'oseh, the one making, from the ordinary verb to do or make; Isaiah 54:5 uses a plural of majesty. The Greek in Hebrews 11:10 is technites, a craftsman, paired with demiourgos.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'asah (H6213) — to do, make, fashion; its participle 'oseh gives maker (Job 4:17; Psalm 95:6; Proverbs 14:31).

Hebrew 'osayik in Isaiah 54:5 — a plural form, thy Makers, a plural of majesty the KJV renders as a singular Maker.

Hebrew bara' (H1254) — to create; used in Scripture only with God as subject, and standing behind the doctrine the title assumes.

Greek technites (G5079) — a craftsman, designer; whose builder and maker is God (Hebrews 11:10).

Greek demiourgos (G1217) — a maker, framer; the second noun in Hebrews 11:10, rendered maker.

Usage

"Let us kneel before the LORD our maker (Psalm 95:6) — the posture of worship argued from the fact of creation."

"He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker (Proverbs 14:31) — social duty grounded in a shared origin."

"Thy Maker is thine husband (Isaiah 54:5) — the Creator’s right joined to the Husband’s covenant."
